comparison: Both evaluate claims about TIM23 core subunit reduction (C3, C51-C54) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes immunoblot data quality with appropriate controls and replicates. Peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'provide compelling evidence' and the editor notes 'evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing.' Complete agreement on this finding.

Both address the surprising finding that most mitochondrial proteins remain unaffected despite reduced TIM23 core levels (C4-C5, C70-C71). Both mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the mechanistic interpretation requires further investigation. Peer Reviewer 2 similarly states 'it remains somewhat unclear why this is,' but both accept the observation itself as a key finding.

Both evaluate the pattern of affected proteins, particularly OXPHOS subunits and MRPs (C78-C81, C86-C87, C131-C132). Both mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the inference about MRP affecting translation is reasonable but would benefit from direct measurement. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'interesting results' without challenge.

Both evaluate OXPHOS functional defects measured by Seahorse (C8-C11, C90-C95) and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes data quality with appropriate sample sizes and statistical analysis. Peer reviewers state 'evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing' and experiments are 'of high quality and sufficiently well-controlled.' Complete agreement.

Both evaluate ATP reduction claims (C12, C108) and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate sample size and statistical analysis. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'compelling evidence' without raising concerns. Complete agreement on this functional consequence.

Both evaluate mitochondrial trafficking defects (C13, C103-C107, C126) and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the ATP-dependence inference is reasonable but not directly proven. Peer reviewers accept the finding as 'interesting results' without challenging the mechanistic interpretation. Both accept the observation and inference.

Both evaluate increased firing rate claims (C15, C115-C117). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED with appropriate data. Peer reviewers also mark as SUPPORTED, explicitly highlighting this as a major finding with 'compelling evidence' for 'increased electrical activity.' Complete agreement.

Both evaluate potassium channel reduction and mechanistic link to firing rate (C16-C17, C118-C119, C121). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, noting pharmacological validation strengthens the link. Peer reviewers also mark as SUPPORTED, describing this as an 'unexpected link between mitochondria and ion channels.' Complete agreement on this major finding.

Both evaluate the link to patient epilepsy phenotype (C18, C127, C136). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting the connection is speculative without patient-derived neuronal data. Peer reviewers mark as SUPPORTED, accepting this as reasonable speculation that 'hints at an unexpected link.' Disagreement on confidence level: OpenEval more cautious, peer reviewers more accepting of the inference.

Both evaluate connections to patient developmental defects and epilepsy (C14, C134-C135). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting these are hypothetical inferences requiring validation. Peer reviewers mark as SUPPORTED, accepting this as 'reasonable speculation' that 'sheds new light' on disease. Disagreement on confidence: OpenEval emphasizes need for validation, peer reviewers accept the speculative interpretation.

Both evaluate the mtDNA copy number control experiment (C88-C89) and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this is an important control for ruling out alternative explanations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of 'sufficiently well-controlled' experiments. Complete agreement.

Both evaluate glycolysis compensation findings (C96-C101) and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the importance of this finding for understanding metabolic consequences. Peer reviewers accept this as part of 'convincing' evidence with 'high quality' experiments. Complete agreement.

Both evaluate negative electrophysiology findings (C109-C114) and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are important controls showing specificity. Peer reviewers accept these as part of the characterization supporting specificity of firing rate effects. Complete agreement on these negative results.

Both evaluate the surprising finding that certain TIM23 complex proteins remain unchanged (C56-C60, C64-C67). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, noting this is a key observation. Peer reviewers also mark as SUPPORTED, explicitly calling this 'surprising' and 'highly interesting.' Complete agreement on this unexpected finding.

Both evaluate the neuronal model recapitulating fibroblast findings (C61-C63). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, noting consistency between model systems strengthens conclusions. Peer reviewers mark as SUPPORTED, noting the use of 'both cells from patients and neurons from mice' as a strength. Complete agreement on validation across systems.

Both address mechanistic interpretations about TIMM50's role (C133). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, noting this is appropriately speculative. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 explicitly stating 'it remains somewhat unclear why this is' and suggesting alternative mechanisms. Disagreement: OpenEval accepts the speculation as reasonable, peer reviewers indicate the mechanism is unresolved.

OpenEval evaluates extensive background knowledge claims (C1-C2, C19-C49) as SUPPORTED, noting these are well-established facts with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers typically focus on novel findings rather than background literature.

OpenEval evaluates neuronal proteomics findings (C7, C82-C87) as SUPPORTED, noting consistency with fibroblast data and appropriate sample size. While peer reviewers accept the overall proteomics approach, no specific peer result addresses this exact set of neuronal proteomics claims in isolation.
